There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page". If your A1c sits in that band, that is the page your AME works from, not this one. Victoza is usually the diabetes product and Saxenda the weight loss one, but your diagnosis is what decides which entry applies to you.

faaStatusDescription: Taken for type 2 diabetes, the FAA's disposition is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA." It records this as "Initial Special Issuance – Requires FAA Decision". That is its listed disposition for "Treated with one or more (non-insulin) diabetic medications". Its Acceptable Combinations chart places liraglutide in Group C (GLP1 mimetics) and says "Use no more than one medication from each group (A-F)", with a 30-day observation when starting a Group B-D medication and 3 days when switching dose or formulation within Group A-D "(including between injectable and oral GLP-1 RA)". Group C is not allowed with Meglitinides.

treatedConditionNote: The FAA's concern is the condition being treated, not the drug. This entry is the weight loss indication, with no diagnosis of diabetes. If you have a diabetes diagnosis, the FAA's diabetes protocol applies to you and not this page. If you take it for prediabetes, insulin resistance or metabolic syndrome, the FAA works from a separate "CACI - Prediabetes Worksheet" covering "Metabolic Syndrome, Impaired Fasting Glucose, Insulin Resistance, Glucose Elevation/Intolerance", with its own Block 60 statement, "CACI qualified prediabetes". faaStatusDescription: "When certification criteria are met", the FAA lists liraglutide under "ACCEPTABLE Weight Loss Medications". It names no brand for it. Its criteria: "A1C must be 6.4 or less with no diagnosis of diabetes", "No history of hypoglycemia requiring intervention", and "Two (2) weeks after starting for weight loss." It also requires "48-hour observation with each dose increase, medication or formulation change." There is a third path the FAA keeps separate: it says "See either the Prediabetes or Weight Loss Management disposition tables", and its worksheet notes "If A1c is in the prediabetic range (5.7 to 6.4%)" to "see the Pre-Diabetes page". If your A1c sits in that band, that is the page your AME works from, not this one. Its Weight Loss Management disposition table is ISSUE on ONE non-insulin diabetic medication component, and on "TWO (2) or more" it is DEFER, "Submit the information to the FAA for a possible Special Issuance". Even the ISSUE is not automatic: it "requires a current, detailed Clinical Progress Note from the treating physician and Hemoglobin A1c lab performed no more than 90 days before the AME exam", or a "Weight Loss Management Status Report". Its CACI worksheet takes "ONLY ONE of the medications listed", says "If the applicant has EVER had an A1C OF 6.5% OR GREATER, DO NOT USE THIS CACI." and that "Diabetes in remission (diet-controlled), diabetes treated with medication (including insulin), or diabetes insipidus DO NOT qualify for this CACI." "Applicants for first or second- class must provide this information annually; applicants for third-class must provide the information with each required exam."
